Verdict. The new engine finds the beat on this mix far more reliably than the old per-visualizer detectors: mean beat F-measure 0.979 over all 13 excerpts (DSP-only fallback 0.818) against 0.584 for the best old detector, and 0.974 on the 4 excerpts that no design decision ever saw. The hybrid engine passed every gate on 13 of 13 excerpts; failures are listed below, not hidden. Live in the app, fired beats land a median 4 ms from the reference and 46 of 54 visualizers passed the live quality check (44 in the first run; re-runs are marked in the table).

1. Architecture

The audio engine and the visuals are now separate systems. Visualizers never touch Web Audio: they are plain renderer modules that receive one shared AudioFrame per animation frame (beats, onsets, bands, spectra, waveforms). The engine owns one AudioContext per session; the complete beat analysis runs on the audio thread at a fixed hop, independent of the render frame rate.

  • Before: 56 components each created their own AudioContext and analysers (two during a crossfade), with six different ad-hoc kick/beat detectors and no tempo tracking.
  • After: one engine, one analysis, predicted beats that fire in the frame they become audible, shared analysers keyed by FFT size/smoothing so every visualizer still reads exactly the data it was tuned on, Auto Gain and AI beat tracking as user toggles.

2. Ground truth

Reference beats come from two independent state-of-the-art offline trackers with unrelated architectures: madmom (RNN + DBN, primary) and beat_this (transformer, ISMIR 2024, cross-check). A 10-second window is scored only when both agree (F ≥ 0.9 at ±70 ms). On the first excerpt madmom's beats lie on a straight 130.01 BPM grid (residual 4.56 ms) and beat_this agrees within 0–10 ms in every window. librosa was tried and rejected: it lost the beat after ~30 s.

The spectrograms confirm the reference: every kick (the typical 150 → 60 Hz pitch drop) starts on a reference beat. They also exposed the hard part of this material — a pickup hit 75 ms before every other beat, rolling basslines that fill the off-beats and loud off-beat hats. Low-frequency onsets are fooled by the pickup and the band above 6 kHz by the hats; that is why the engine takes its beat phase from the 150 Hz – 6 kHz band.

Reference evidence plots

3. Beat accuracy on the mix

Each excerpt is streamed causally in 128-sample blocks — exactly as the AudioWorklet receives audio — at 44.1 and 48 kHz. Scores cover the unambiguous windows after a 5 s warm-up. The four detectors the old visualizers used are replayed on the same audio through an emulated AnalyserNode at 60 fps. F = F-measure at ±70 ms; AMLt = continuity allowing off-beat/double/half metrical levels. Gates: F ≥ 0.80, AMLt ≥ 0.90, tempo correct in ≥ 90 % of windows, |median offset| ≤ 20 ms, clearly better than the old code.

Timing of detected beats

Signed offset of matched beats (hybrid, 44.1 kHz, all excerpts), 5 ms bins from −70 to +70 ms. The clock is predictive: beats are emitted at the predicted time, not one detection delay later.

AI beat tracking

Every ~5 s (2.5 s while settling) the network looks at the last 10 s and the arbiter decides: 296 confirms (clock on the beat; the DSP may not jump phase for 12 s), 8 metrical phase shifts, 0 octave re-timings and 47 abstentions (too few or inconsistent beats) over 13 excerpt runs. Inference averaged 1026 ms per 10 s window (WebAssembly, one thread, in Node; about 1 s in Chrome on this machine), in a Worker off the audio and render threads.

Front-end parity with beat_this in Python (same audio, same model): log-mel mean absolute difference 0.009 (mean level 3.84), frame lag 0, and 21/21 beat peaks identical within one 20 ms frame.

Beat lock: modulation depth of the frame motion (or luminance) folded onto the reference beat grid, relative to grids in which every beat is independently jittered by up to half a period (1.00 = no locking; * = p < 0.05, 200 draws). Phase-agnostic, so a smoothed or delayed reaction still counts. Audio r: strongest correlation between a visual feature (luminance, motion) and an audio feature (level, bass, lit spectrum, kick envelope) in 250 ms bins; * = significant under a circular-shift permutation test that takes the same maximum over all 8 pairs. Rules: beat-driven visualizers need beat lock ≥ 1.3×; continuous ones beat lock ≥ 1.1× or |r| ≥ 0.25 (both significant); all must render, move and log no errors. Fired-beat F scores the frames in which the visualizer received isBeat against the reference (±70 ms); at low frame rates a frame simply lasts longer than the tolerance. Visualizers that failed the first 20 s run were measured again over 40 s (70–118 s, including the break and the drop), after the fixes to Fireworks Show and MS Defrag and with an uploaded image for the upload-driven visualizers; both verdicts are shown. FPS measured with the probe's canvas read-back switched off. Renderer: ANGLE (Intel, Mesa Intel(R) Graphics (ADL-N), OpenGL ES 3.2).

Deep dive: ten beat-heavy visualizers, three sections of the mix

Curves: frame-to-frame motion folded onto the reference beats (0 = the beat, 0.5 = half-way), relative to its mean. A flat line at 1 means the picture ignores the beat; a peak means it moves on the beat. Snapshots were captured in the exact render frame in which a beat fired, and half-way between beats.

steady groovepickup sectionbreak → drop

Before vs after

The deep-dive visualizers plus the slow and weakly reacting ones, in the old app (build of main) and the new app, fed the same audio through the Microphone path (Chrome fake capture) and measured by the same injected frame probe. Value: peak of the beat-aligned motion response (best 150 ms window between −100 and +250 ms, relative to the mean; 1.00 = none) and its lag. The fake-capture start is only known to within some tens of milliseconds, so the lags share an unknown common offset — but the difference between before and after is meaningful: the old bass detectors respond 80–100 ms before the beat grid (they fire on the pickup hit that precedes every other beat), the new engine's beats respond after it. Frame rates are identical before and after for the slow visualizers (their cost is their own drawing, e.g. large canvas shadow blurs), so low frame rates are not a regression.

5. The new-visualizer skill

Following .github/skills/adding-visualizer/SKILL.md end to end: npm run new:viz -- skilltest "Skill Test" --template canvas2d --beat produced a module and registry entry that passed lint, the unit tests, the e2e mount test and the live quality check out of the box (beat lock x4.61, p=0.005; correlation with the music 0.78; 60 fps; no errors). The three.js and shader templates were also generated with and without --beat and type-checked. The throwaway visualizer was removed afterwards.

6. Known limitations

  • DSP-only mode (AI beat tracking off or unavailable) still locks onto the off-beat or a pickup in some rolling-bass sections (see the DSP columns); the neural arbiter exists for exactly these cases.
  • The network runs every ~5 s on a 10 s window; after a start or a hard cut the beat can take several seconds to become confident (the report's live runs start mid-song).
  • Slow music (< 90 BPM) is tracked at double time by design (dance-music tempo prior); the beat stays in time.
  • Frame rates depend on the GPU. On the integrated GPU used here several visualizers run below 30 fps in both the old and the new app (e.g. Sheet Music ~8, Fractal Orb ~9, Neon Hex Tunnel ~12, Tunnel ~17, Cyber City ~19): their cost is their own drawing (large canvas shadow blurs, raymarched shaders). Replacing canvas shadowBlur with a cheaper glow would help a lot but changes the look, so it was left for a follow-up.
  • 8 visualizers do not meet the live criteria: glitchbackground, sheetmusic, tunnel, particlesstream, fluidsmoke, msdefrag, shambhala, glitchbackgroundsendspin. They render without errors, but within 20–40 s of music their picture either reacts in ways this measurement cannot resolve (random glitch triggers, slow block-by-block animation, few frames per second) or reacts weakly; the before/after measurements show the same behaviour in the old app.
  • Some visualizers keep pre-existing quirks on purpose (unchanged look), e.g. audio-modulated speeds multiplied by elapsed time in AnunakiSphere, AuroraWaves, CyberCity, Shambhala and HexGlobe clouds.

7. Reproduce

npm run eval:prepare (downloads the mix, cuts excerpts) · uv run scripts/eval/reference.py … (reference beats) · npm run eval:mix · npm run test:unit · npm test · npm run eval:live (dev server on :3101) · npm run eval:before-after · npm run report. Heavy jobs were run under a memory cap (systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=…).
